title: Chapter 132 – The Glass Basin
html:
[Western Basin – Lin Jian]

The Pass of Seven Winds is open for a hundred and nine days, and Jian uses all of them.

He sets out on the second morning of summer, with a pack of dried curd and a skin of fermented milk and a felt cloak that Odgerel's wife has stitched with her own hands. Temur walks him to the first cairn. The boy is nine now, taller than he was, with a lump of coal in his fist and a new tooth coming in crooked. He does not weep. He holds out a flat piece of slate, scratched over with black marks.

"I wrote it myself," he says gruffly. "In the winter. It says what you said. A name given back cannot be taken."

Jian takes the slate. He reads it. The characters are crooked and the third is backwards.

"It is perfect," he says.

"It is not."

"It is the best thing anyone has given me in ten years." He wraps it in felt and tucks it inside his tunic, beside the spoon. "Keep writing, Temur. Write every name you hear. Someday it will matter."

"Why?"

"Because you will be the only one who can."

The boy stares at him. Then he nods, once, the solemn nod of the very young, and runs back down the hill without looking round. Behind Jian, in a line along the snow, the Unkept rise one by one from their kneeling, and follow.

* * *

The pass is a mile-wide trough of blue ice, pocked with meltwater lakes and floored with shattered rock.

It is the most beautiful place he has ever been, and the most dangerous. The walls rise on either side for thousands of feet, sheer and fluted, hung with icicles the size of towers. The sky overhead is a thin cold blue. In the middle of the trough a river of meltwater runs, bright as quicksilver, over a bed of green-black stone, and every few hundred paces there is a crack in the ice that opens down into a bottomless darkness. Pebble rides on his shoulder with her whiskers frozen stiff.

"Left," she says. "Always left. The right ones are hollow."

"How hollow?"

"The kind you fall into."

He keeps to the left. For eleven days they follow the river, sleeping in snow caves, living on the dried curd, drinking meltwater so cold it makes his teeth ache. The Unkept come behind in single file, silent, their rags stiff with ice. On the sixth night one of them does not get up. Jian goes to him in the dark and finds him sitting against a boulder with his head bowed and his hands in his lap, rime on his lashes, dead. There is a faint, awful smile on the wasted face.

They bury him in a crevasse, with a stone on his chest. The Nameless says the oldest word, the hooked one, in a voice no louder than a breath. Jian says nothing. He has no name to give.

On the ninth day the ice speaks.

It begins as a low groan, like a beast clearing its throat, and Pebble has her claws in his shoulder before he hears it. He looks up. High on the eastern wall, a hundred stories above, a vast white shelf has come loose from the cliff and is sliding, slowly, almost gracefully, into the air.

"Run," says Pebble, very calmly.

He runs. Behind him the Unkept break in all directions, silent, like startled birds. The roar comes down on them like the end of the world, a wall of snow and shattered ice the height of a hill, and the air in front of it turns white and solid and hits him in the back like a hand. He is thrown flat. The light goes out.

It is the Door that saves him. He does not choose it. He feels the cold plane open under his ribs, feels a thin bright line of seam shining in the dark a few paces off, and he is through before he knows he has moved, four units and a fold of nothing, and stands gasping on a ledge of black rock, thirty paces to the side, watching the avalanche thunder past below him and fill the trough from wall to wall.

When it settles, the silence is absolute.

Fourteen of the Unkept come out of the snow, one at a time, coughing, brushing rime from their rags. They stand in a ragged line. They count themselves without speaking.

Five are missing.

He sits on the ledge a long time with his arms around his knees. In the dark of his mind, where the drawer is, something small and bright has just gone out. He tries to find it, and cannot. He remembers the avalanche. He remembers Pebble's voice. He does not remember what he was thinking about, on the morning before, as he climbed.

They dig for three hours. They find two. The other three are under forty feet of ice, and the Nameless, who has dug longest and hardest, stands at last with his hands bleeding and his blank face turned to the white wall.

"There are no names to put on them," he says.

"I know."

"I should have liked to." A pause. "It is a small thing to wish."

Jian says nothing. He puts a stone on the snow where the three lie, and sits beside it for an hour, and then they go on.

At the highest point of the pass, on the twelfth day, the whole world falls away.

* * *

The western slope drops in a series of enormous steps, white and gold and green, toward a plain so wide that its far edge dissolves into the sky. And in the middle of the plain, ringed with mountains, lies a lake of glass.

That is what it looks like. A circle forty miles across, perfectly flat, perfectly smooth, catching the sun and throwing it back in a single blinding sheet. There is no water in it. There is no ice. There is only a plain of fused sand, black and green and amber, as if some titanic fire had come down from the sky and melted the earth into a mirror. Along its rim, tiny as grains of rice, lies a scatter of buildings.

"The Glass Basin," says a voice behind him.

It is a woman, hooded, thin, with a staff and a pack, who has been following them down the slope for an hour. She is perhaps sixty. She wears a shapeless gray traveler's cloak, and her face, under the hood, is lined and brown and calm. She does not seem surprised to see nineteen ragged men in single file behind a gray-haired stranger.

"Forgive me," she says. "I do not wish to be a nuisance. I am a reader of the Basin. We are told when someone comes down from the pass." She inclines her head. "My teacher said the eighth would walk down carrying a stone spoon, with a small gray beast on his shoulder."

Jian touches his breast. The spoon is wood.

"It is not stone."

"Ah." The woman smiles. "My teacher was old."

"What is your teacher's name?"

"Hai." She shifts the staff. "It is a short name. It means the sea. He died on the tenth of last winter, and asked me to wait for you at the top of the slope. I have been here four months. I was beginning to think he was wrong."

"And what are you?"

"I am the last of the Quiet School." She lifts her hood back, showing close-cropped gray hair, and eyes like a still pond. "We keep the lamp."

* * *

It takes them three days to cross the glass.

The reader leads. She walks with her staff and her wide-brimmed hat, tapping each step, and they follow in a long line, with their cloaks pulled over their faces against the glare. The heat is extraordinary. The plain gives it back from below as the sun pours it down from above, so that a man seems to walk on the inside of a furnace. Water goes fast. Pebble gasps under his collar. The Unkept, who do not eat or drink, plod on without complaint, their rags smoking in the heat.

At noon on the second day, the glass begins to show him things.

He sees a street. Not a mirage; it is too sharp, too still. A narrow paved lane between rows of flat-roofed houses, going away from him across the plain, with a cart standing in it, and a woman on the step of a doorway, half turned, a basket on her hip. She is not moving. She is not alive. She is a shape in the glass, caught at the instant of the fire, and she is looking at something just past his shoulder with an expression of mild surprise.

He stops.

"Do not look too long," says Lan Ji, without turning. "It is not kind."

"How many are there?"

"Seven thousand. We have not found them all." She taps on. "My teacher said you get used to it. I have not. I stop at every one. I say the name, if I know it. Most I do not."

He walks on. He sees a child with a kite. He sees an old man with a pipe. He sees a dog, a dozen dogs, running in a pack, caught in mid-leap. He sees a girl of perhaps seventeen, kneeling at a well, her hand raised to her mouth, her hair streaming back, and he understands that she was looking up, at the sky, at the instant that it opened.

Pebble has gone silent on his shoulder.

"They are not suffering," she says at last. "I thought they might be. They are not. They are only... stopped." A pause. "It is very much like a seam. A place where the counting stopped."

"Is that better?"

"I don't know." Her voice is small. "I think it is worse."

* * *

The Quiet School is a village of glass.

It sits on the very edge of the basin, where the fused plain meets the living rock, a cluster of sixty low houses built from blocks of green-black obsidian, joined with white mortar, roofed with turf. They shine in the afternoon sun like jewels. There are gardens between them, small and fierce, planted in boxes of imported earth. There are children. There are goats. A bell rings somewhere, a plain iron bell, and from the doors people come out one by one to look at the strangers, and stop, and fall silent.

"We are not many," says the reader, whose name is Lan Ji. "Two hundred and nine. We are the grandchildren of grandchildren of the first school. The fourth Operator taught us to read the glass."

"The glass?"

"The Basin is not natural." She leads him down a lane between the houses, with her staff tapping on the polished stone. "Six hundred years ago, there was a city here. Seven thousand people. Then the sky opened and a light came down, and the whole city became this." She gestures at the endless gleaming plain. "The fourth Operator walked out of the ashes the next morning. He sat down in the middle of the glass and began to count the people. There were nine survivors."

"He saved them?"

"He taught them. That is different." Her smile is slight. "He showed them how to read what was left. In the glass, you see, there are faces. And words. And sounds. The light did not only melt the sand. It remembered. If you set your ear to the Basin on a still night, you can hear the city talking. Seven thousand voices, all at once, endlessly." She stops at the door of a low house. "He said it was the saddest and most beautiful thing he had ever heard. He stayed for forty years to listen."

"Forty years."

"He died here. He is buried under the school." She opens the door. "But before he died, he built a room for you."

* * *

They feed him that night in the long hall, at a table of black glass, and the children come to look.

There are forty of them, ranging from toddlers to gangling twelve-year-olds, all with the same still, attentive faces as their teacher. They sit cross-legged on the floor in a half-circle, with their bowls on their knees, and watch him eat. He is aware of the Unkept in the doorway, motionless, a row of gray scarecrows, and of the Nameless standing apart with its blank face turned to the wall. He is aware that nobody in the room is afraid.

"Is it true," says a small girl of eight, "that you can walk through air?"

"Who told you that?"

"The glass."

He glances at Lan Ji. The reader's face is perfectly serene. "They listen from the cradle," she says. "It is not a gift. It is a habit."

"What does it say about me?"

"That you are tired," says the girl solemnly. "And that you have lost things. And that someone is very sorry." She considers. "It does not say who."

A boy of ten, thin and freckled, puts down his bowl. "I can play it for you," he says. "If you like. The city. Just a little."

"Please."

They take him out onto the glass.

It is dusk, and the plain is a sheet of molten gold, stretching to the end of the world. The children lead him out a hundred paces from the edge and make him lie down on his back, with his ear against the polished surface, which is warm from the day and faintly trembling. The Nameless stands at the rim. The reader kneels at his head. Pebble sits on his chest with her eyes shut.

"Listen," says the boy.

For a long time there is nothing. Then, from very deep, from a great way beneath his ear, there rises a sound. It is not music. It is not speech. It is the sound of a crowd, the way a crowd sounds from the far side of a hill, a thick warm hum of ten thousand overlapping voices, murmuring, laughing, arguing, bargaining. A baby cries. A woman calls a name. A dog barks. Somewhere a bell is ringing, a plain bright iron bell, and a man's voice says, quite clearly, Be careful with that, it's hot.

Then the bell rings once more, and everything stops.

He lies there, with the stars coming out, and tears running down into his ears, and a thousand years of silence rushing in over the plain. The boy touches his shoulder, very gently.

"That is how it ends," he says. "Every night. We don't know why."

"I know why," says Jian.

"Why?"

"Because someone pressed a button."

The boy does not understand. He nods anyway, politely, and lies down beside him in the warm glass, and they listen to the silence together.

* * *

On their third night in the school, the Nameless comes to the door of the guest-house.

It is late. Jian is sitting at the low table in the lamplight, with a cup of the reader's bitter tea going cold at his elbow and Temur's slate propped against the wall. He hears no step. He looks up, and the blank gray figure is standing in the doorway, one pace inside the threshold, with its hands at its sides.

"You are not supposed to enter," says Jian.

"I am not entering. I am standing in the door." The voice is mild. "There is a distinction. I think the sender would approve."

"What do you want?"

"To say something. And then to go away." A pause. "I was a Number for forty-one years. I was taken at nineteen. I remember the day, the Keeper's hand on my head, the smell of the burning paper. I remember the first night. I remember thinking, I will remember my name." The head tilts. "I did, for a year. Then it began to slip."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be. It is a very ordinary sorrow." The thin voice is steady. "What I wished to say is that I have been listening to the glass. At night. While you sleep." He raises one hand, slowly, and lays it flat on his own chest. "There is a name in it. Not many. Perhaps four or five, among the seven thousand. And one of them, when the wind is right, sounds as if it were mine."

Jian sits quite still.

"It is a name I have never heard," says the Nameless. "I cannot say it. I cannot even hold it in my head. But it rhymes with something. Something in the center of me, where the hole is. It is like a key that does not fit and yet turns." He lowers his hand. "I do not know why I am telling you. I think I wished to say it aloud to someone who would not be kind."

"I can be kind."

"Please do not." The faintest trace of a laugh. "I could not bear it."

He bows, very slightly, and withdraws up the stair, and is gone. Jian sits there in the blue light, listening to his steps dwindle away through the stacks, and for the first time since the Sect he finds that he cannot make himself believe, entirely, that the man in gray is an enemy.

* * *

Pebble finds him at the table at dawn, still awake.

She leaps onto the stone with the little bell chiming, and sits on the corner of the table with her tail curled round her paws, and studies him for some time with her head on one side.

"You have not slept."

"No."

"You are thinking about the Door."

"I am thinking about sixty percent." He rubs his eyes. "The Seal is at sixty-five. Every Dock I wake on the Door costs six. If the next one asks the same, I will be at fifty-nine, and I do not know what the Cole door does below sixty." He laughs under his breath. "Three years ago I would have been terrified."

"And now?"

"Now I am merely tired." He looks at her. "Do you know what is on the other side of the door? Page Two?"

"No." She is quiet. "But I know what the Door is afraid of."

"The Door is afraid?"

"The way a lock is afraid of a key." She stirs. "It was made to open. It wants to open. But it was also made to be opened only by someone who could bear what was inside. You have been paying it, a bit at a time, in small things. Each step. Each draw. It has been counting you." Her eyes are steady. "It is not cruel. It is being careful. It will not give you Page Two until it is sure you can pay."

"And if I never can?"

"Then it will wait." The little beast yawns. "It is very good at waiting. It is the best thing it does."

* * *

Dock Four lies beneath the school's library, down a stair of black glass.

The reader leads him through the stacks, past long shelves of rolled paper and small glass tablets etched with fine writing, to a plain wooden door at the back of a storeroom. Beyond it, a flight of steps winds down into the dark. The air that comes up is cold and still and smells of dust and old iron.

"We have kept it clean," Lan Ji says. "Every spring, every school-child sweeps it. Nobody goes in. It is the one rule of the school. It is carved over the door." She lifts the lantern, and in its light Jian reads the inscription, cut deep into the black lintel in a small cramped hand.

Do not touch the lamp until he comes.

He stands for a long time looking at the words. There is no signature. There does not need to be.

"He knew," he says quietly.

"He knew everything," says Lan Ji. "That was his tragedy. He died in his bed at seventy-one, surrounded by pupils, with a smile on his face. And the last thing he said was, I am so sorry. I was happy, and I was not supposed to be."

"There is one more thing," says Lan Ji, lowering her voice. "My teacher told it to me on the day he died, and I have never told it to anyone. On the night the fourth Operator died, two men came to the school. Strangers, in gray, with plum-colored seals at their collars. They did not speak. They stood at the door of his house, and the pupils let them in, because the old man had said to. They sat with him until dawn. And when he stopped breathing, they lifted his body onto a litter and carried it up the slope, toward the pass."

"Toward the Gate."

"Toward something. We did not follow." Her hands tighten on the staff. "They left a bowl of water by his bed. It was untouched. Whatever they came for, they took it. And the next morning, there was a new grave in the school yard, with his name on it, and nothing in it but a folded cloak."

"A grave with nothing in it."

"A grave for the memory of him. We buried the cloak." She meets his eyes. "I think the body was never ours."

The lantern flickers. From somewhere far down the stair comes a sound like a very long exhalation, the sigh of an old house when the door is opened after a hundred years.

Jian takes the lantern from her hand. He steps onto the first stair.

* * *

The Dock is exactly like the first.

Low, square, dark green. A desk. A stool. A cot. A cup. The dust lies undisturbed, a skin like paint. But this room has been lived in more thoroughly; the walls are lined with shelves, and the shelves with small glass tablets, a hundred, a thousand, each of them etched in the same cramped blue-black hand. A woven mat lies on the floor. In the corner stands a child's wooden toy, a little horse with a missing leg, set carefully on a ledge as if it were sleeping.

He crosses the room. He lays his palm on the wall.

```
DOCK — ARK-4
Status: DARK
Wake: 30 CE (carry 12 / 12)
Door-fed: Seal -6% (now 65 → 59)
WARNING: Below 60%, the Cole door will not open
further pages until Seal ≥ 60%.
Recovery: ~1% per month.
```

He reads it, and reads it again.

There it is: the cost. Not a fortune, not a memory, but time. A year of waiting, a year in which Page Two of the Cole door will stay shut, while he sits in a room under a school of glass and learns everything this man left behind. He thinks of the Gate. He thinks of the Chain. He thinks of a ninth sleeper breathing, and a spoon, and a bell.

A year, he thinks. I have given more for less.

He closes his eyes and lets the Door widen.

* * *

The lamp that wakes is blue.

He sees it as a pale blue ball of light above a brass wick, cold and clean and steady, and the shadows leap to meet it. The shelves glow. The glass tablets come alive one by one, a thousand points of faint blue fire, like a field of stars seen through ice. Lan Ji, at the door, makes a small hushed sound.

On the desk, under a flat black stone, lies a single sheet of paper. It is creased down the middle.

To whoever comes after.

He picks it up. His hands are shaking.

My name is Ethan Cole. I am the fourth Operator of this Dock. I have been here forty years.

I did not go through the Gate.

I want you to understand that. I decided, on the first day, that I would not. I decided that if the voice said HOME, I would say no. I would find a way to stay. I would build a school, and marry no one, and grow old, and be useful. I would die in this world and be buried in it. I thought that if I could just refuse, the loop would break.

It did not break. I am sorry.

I have written this log so that you will know how it ends. Read it slowly. It is the saddest thing I have ever done.

Below, in the dark blue ink that glistens like fresh paint, in the same hand but sharper, newer, impatient:

Lin Jian. Page 1 of 40. You will want to skip ahead. Do not.

—E.C.

The lamp burns on, blue and cold. And in the corner, on the ledge, the little wooden horse with the missing leg seems to turn its head, ever so slightly, to watch him read.
